*   $R, \mathbf{t}$: Camera extrinsics [S1].

The claim states that $R$ and $t$ represent camera extrinsics. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly defines the transformation of a voxel center into the camera frame using the formula $p_c = R^T (p - t)$, where $R$ is rotation and $t$ is translation. In computer vision and 3D reconstruction contexts, the rotation matrix $R$ and translation vector $t$ that transform points from the global/world frame to the camera frame are the standard definition of camera extrinsics. The text refers to 'camera pose (R, t)' and uses them for projecting voxels into the camera frame, which confirms they are the extrinsic parameters.
supported
It builds on the weighted averaging fusion technique by Curless and Levoy [Curless and Levoy 1996] [S1].

The claim states that the method builds on the weighted averaging fusion technique by Curless and Levoy [1996]. The provided text explicitly states: 'With multiple calibrated views, each view produces a per-voxel TSDF measurement, and valid measurements are fused by weighted averaging into the global TSDF volume [Curless and Levoy 1996].' This confirms that the weighted averaging fusion technique from Curless and Levoy is used in the described method.

Projective TSDF Fusion computes signed distance values for voxels from calibrated depth images by projecting voxel centers into the camera frame and comparing projected depth with observed depth [S1].

The claim states that Projective TSDF Fusion computes signed distance values for voxels from calibrated depth images by projecting voxel centers into the camera frame and comparing projected depth with observed depth. The provided evidence (Source [S1] passages and notes) explicitly describes this exact process: transforming voxel centers to the camera frame, projecting them to 2D image coordinates, reading the observed depth, and computing the signed distance as the difference between observed and projected depth. All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
